title: What Coffee Actually Does to Your Body
description:
Coffee doesn't add energy to your body. It hides a tiredness signal your brain has been collecting all day. Follow one cup from the first sip to hours later, and see why the same coffee hits everyone differently.

Sources:
- U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine is Too Much?: https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much
- MedlinePlus, Caffeine: https://medlineplus.gov/caffeine.html
- Current Neuropharmacology (2015), Caffeine: Cognitive and Physical Performance Enhancer or Psychoactive Drug?: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4462044/
- Nutrients (2021), Caffeine as a Factor Influencing the Functioning of the Human Body: Friend or Foe?: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8467199
- NHLBI, How Sleep Works: Your Sleep/Wake Cycle: https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep/sleep-wake-cycle
- ScienceDaily (2009), NIH-funded study on astrocytes, adenosine and sleep pressure: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/01/090128122814.htm

This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice.

scenes.narration: Coffee doesn't actually give you energy. What it does is sneakier. It blocks the signal telling your brain how tired you are.
scenes.headline: COFFEE ISN'T ENERGY

visual.query: cup of black coffee on table
visual.note: steaming cup of black coffee on a wooden table

scenes.narration: The star of your cup is caffeine, and coffee doesn't own it. Caffeine occurs naturally in more than sixty plants, including tea leaves, kola nuts, and the cacao pods that give us chocolate.
scenes.headline: FOUND IN SIXTY-PLUS PLANTS

visual.query: coffee beans tea leaves cacao pods
visual.note: coffee beans, tea leaves, and cacao side by side

scenes.narration: And we take in a lot of it. One review estimates the average person worldwide gets about seventy-six milligrams of caffeine a day. In the United States and Canada, it's closer to two hundred ten to two hundred thirty-eight.
scenes.headline: NORTH AMERICA LOVES CAFFEINE
scenes.sub: About three times the world average

visual.note: people lined up at a coffee shop counter

scenes.narration: Start with the first sip. Caffeine is absorbed quickly from your gut into your bloodstream. From there it spreads into nearly every tissue in your body, and it slips easily past the barrier that protects your brain.
scenes.headline: STRAIGHT TO YOUR BRAIN

visual.spec: path of caffeine: mouth, stomach and small intestine, bloodstream, then crossing the blood-brain barrier into the brain

scenes.narration: Caffeine levels in your blood usually peak within about an hour. Many studies put it at thirty to sixty minutes, but it can range from fifteen minutes to two hours, depending on your body and whether you've just eaten.
scenes.headline: THE PEAK HITS FAST

visual.spec: line graph of caffeine level in blood over time: rising to a peak around thirty to sixty minutes, shaded range from fifteen minutes to two hours, then slowly declining

scenes.narration: To see what it does next, meet adenosine. While you're awake, this chemical gradually builds up in your brain. The more it accumulates, the stronger your urge to sleep. Scientists call this sleep pressure, and NIH-funded research in mice suggests support cells called astrocytes help release it.
scenes.headline: MEET ADENOSINE

scenes.narration: Adenosine works by docking onto receptors on your brain cells, like a key in a lock. Caffeine fits into those same locks without turning them. It blocks the receptors, so the tiredness message can't get through.
scenes.headline: A KEY THAT BLOCKS THE LOCK

visual.spec: brain cell receptor shown as a lock; adenosine key fits and sends a tired signal; caffeine key fits but blocks the signal, so the receptor stays quiet

scenes.narration: With that brake released, your brain releases more of its own stimulating chemicals, like dopamine and noradrenaline. You feel more alert and awake. But caffeine doesn't stop adenosine from building up. It only hides the signal.
scenes.headline: THE BRAKES COME OFF

visual.query: woman working alert at laptop with coffee
visual.note: focused person working at a laptop with a coffee mug

scenes.narration: The rest of your body notices too. Caffeine can raise your blood pressure. It increases the acid your stomach releases, which can lead to heartburn for some people. And it's a diuretic, so your body sends out more water.
scenes.headline: IT'S NOT JUST YOUR BRAIN

visual.note: simple anatomy illustration of the stomach and digestive tract

scenes.narration: How long does it last? The effects can linger for four to six hours. Caffeine's half-life, the time your body needs to clear half of it, is often three to five hours, but it ranges from about two to twelve. That means an afternoon cup can still be circulating at bedtime.
scenes.headline: HOW LONG IT LINGERS
scenes.sub: Effects can last four to six hours

visual.note: office desk in afternoon light, suggesting hours passing

scenes.narration: Why such a huge range? Your liver does most of the work of breaking caffeine down, and its pace varies from person to person. Smokers clear caffeine almost twice as fast as nonsmokers, while pregnancy slows clearance down.
scenes.headline: YOUR LIVER SETS THE PACE

visual.note: clean anatomical illustration of the liver

scenes.narration: That's why the same cup can leave one person buzzing and another ready for a nap. The FDA notes wide variation in how sensitive people are to caffeine and how quickly they get rid of it.
scenes.headline: SAME CUP, DIFFERENT EFFECT

visual.note: two people sharing coffee, one energetic, one relaxed

scenes.narration: How much caffeine is in a cup varies a lot too. MedlinePlus lists about ninety-five to two hundred milligrams in an eight-ounce cup of coffee. Even decaf usually has two to fifteen. And for context, the FDA cites four hundred milligrams a day as an amount not generally linked to negative effects in healthy adults.
scenes.headline: WHAT'S IN A CUP?
scenes.sub: It varies more than you think

visual.note: coffee being poured from a drip machine into a mug

scenes.narration: The FDA also notes that too much caffeine can bring on a racing heart, anxiety, trouble sleeping, and headaches. Regular drinkers who suddenly go without may notice headaches, drowsiness, and irritability, which usually fade after a couple of days.
scenes.headline: WHEN THE BODY PUSHES BACK

visual.query: tired man rubbing eyes at desk
visual.note: person rubbing their eyes, looking tired

scenes.narration: And when caffeine finally wears off, adenosine can reach its receptors again. The sleep pressure that kept building all day is still there, waiting. So coffee isn't fuel. It's more like tape over a warning light.
scenes.headline: TAPE OVER A WARNING LIGHT

visual.note: empty mug by a window at dusk

scenes.narration: Follow Inside Your Body for more of the science of you.
